articles.title: Renewable energy in NI reaches record level
articles.summary: And for the first time renewable generation has consistently exceeded non-renewable generation since January.
articles.content:
More than half (53%) of Northern Ireland's electricity came from renewable sources in the year to June – beating the level previously set in 2022.

And for the first time renewable generation has consistently exceeded non-renewable generation since January.

Even when imported electricity was taken into account, the amount of renewables equalled the previous record of 50%, set in 2022/23.

The Economy Minister Caoimhe Archibald said the increasing level of renewable energy would help Northern Ireland "move away from price volatility and towards more stable and fairer prices" .

Almost three-quarters (74%) of renewable electricity came from wind. Bioenergy – anaerobic digestion, incineration and fermentation – provided just under one-fifth (18%).

Solar energy provided 6%, landfill gas provided 1%, and hydro/tidal generation provided 1%.

Northern Ireland has a target of generating 80% of electricity from renewable sources by 2030.

The increase to 53% to June 2026 follows several years of reduced renewable generation.

Lower levels can be due to weather conditions.

There is also a high rate of dispatch down in Northern Ireland – when turbines are switched off because there is not enough demand for the power being generated.

That is to protect the grid which has a limit on the amount of renewable energy it can carry due to fluctuations.

But moving to more renewable energy is a critical part of the journey to net zero and the transition from fossil fuels.

The minister said the rising cost of fossil fuels globally was "impacting negatively" on both businesses and households, particularly those with lower incomes.

She added that increased levels of renewable electricity "move us away from price volatility and towards more stable and fairer prices for the electricity we use".
articles.reasoning: The article reports a significant and measurable increase in renewable energy generation in Northern Ireland, with renewables surpassing non-renewables for the first time consistently. This represents meaningful progress toward climate action and energy stability, benefiting society broadly by reducing reliance on fossil fuels and stabilizing energy prices.

Since January, renewable energy has consistently produced more electricity than non-renewable sources like coal or gas. **Impact** – This is the first time renewables have regularly outpaced fossil fuels in Northern Ireland, showing real progress in clean energy use. articles.title: Officer to combat homes pumping sewage into rivers
articles.summary: Misconnections happen when incorrectly installed plumbing allows waste water to be diverted to surface drains.
articles.content:
A dedicated officer is to be hired in west London in a trial to combat the problem of water-polluting misconnections.

Owing to incorrect plumbing, affected households pump waste into surface drains, which can then spread, killing wildlife and damaging waterways.

Misconnections are illegal, and fixing them is the responsibility of the property owner, external.

Local authorities can take enforcement action, and if the pilot - funded by the mayor of London's office - is successful, the measure could be rolled out across the capital.

Funding is to be spent where the issue is considered a particular problem, including the River Brent catchment area.

Founder of the volunteer group Clean Up the River Brent (CURB), Ben Morris, said there was "good reason" to think misconnections "are the biggest single cause of pollution in London's rivers".

He added: "We need to see stronger action from the councils to get this done.

"They have the power of enforcement and they need to be using those powers to get those property owners to sort out the misconnections."
articles.reasoning: The article describes a proactive environmental initiative funded by the mayor's office to hire a dedicated officer to address illegal sewage misconnections that pollute rivers, which has broad positive impact on water quality, wildlife, and public health in London. The pilot program, if successful, could be expanded city-wide, indicating significant scope and substance.

**One-sentence takeaway** – London is testing a new officer role to stop illegal sewage leaks from homes, aiming to protect rivers and wildlife by fixing plumbing mistakes.

articles.title: 'Miracle' eagle with broken wing spotted back above Scottish coast
articles.summary: A sea eagle that confounded experts by surviving with a broken wing has been spotted back above Scotland's west coast.
articles.content:
A sea eagle that confounded experts by surviving into adulthood with a badly broken wing has been spotted back in the skies above Scotland's west coast.

The bird was dubbed the Isle of Mull's "miracle eagle" by charity the RSPB after it fell from its nest as a chick during a storm in 2023.

Experts that monitor the island's sea eagle population did not expect the male chick to survive, but it has now been spotted three years on - soaring above the island with the distinctive kink in its wing clearly visible.

Retired RSPB officer Dave Sexton, whose has worked with the island's sea eagles for more than 20 years, described the sighting as "incredible".
articles.reasoning: The story reports a sea eagle surviving and thriving despite a severe injury, highlighting successful wildlife resilience and conservation efforts with broad environmental significance.

**Context** – A sea eagle chick fell from its nest during a storm on Scotland’s Isle of Mull in 2023. The fall caused a severe break in one of its wings, and experts believed the bird would not survive.

**What happened** – Despite the injury, the sea eagle, called the “miracle eagle” by the conservation group RSPB, has been seen flying again above Scotland’s west coast. The bird is now three years old, and its damaged wing is still visible as it soars over the island.

**Impact** – This sighting is remarkable because most birds with such serious wing injuries cannot fly or survive in the wild. The eagle’s survival shows how strong and resilient wildlife can be when supported by conservation efforts. It also gives hope for protecting other injured animals.

**What’s next step** – Experts will continue to watch the eagle and the island’s sea eagle population to learn more about how injured birds can live and thrive. The story may help improve ways to protect and care for wildlife in the future.

**One-sentence takeaway** – A sea eagle with a badly broken wing has defied expectations by surviving and flying again above Scotland’s Isle of Mull.

articles.title: Pygmy raccoons teach each other to make toys out of paper and sand
articles.summary: Critically endangered pygmy raccoons on Cozumel Island in Mexico have shown remarkable creativity by making balls out of rubbish at beach clubs
articles.content:
A pygmy raccoon holding a handmade toy ball Nessie O'Neil

Young pygmy raccoons on a Mexican island have been seen teaching each other to make toy balls out of rubbish, in a rare example of animals crafting objects purely for playing with.

“My first reaction was, oh my gosh, that’s absolutely adorable!” says Nessie O’Neil at Miami University in Ohio, who is researching the impact of tourism on the critically endangered pygmy raccoons (Procyon pygmaeus) of Cozumel Island.

O’Neil filmed as one of the younger raccoons fished paper out of a rubbish bin, dipped it in a bowl of water and rolled it in sand, making a ball.

Advertisement

Over days of observation, she recorded the creatures as they made more balls and used them to play “football” with other raccoons and dwarf coatis (Nasua narica nelsoni), another raccoon-like animal. Siblings taught each other the ball-making procedure, and even tried to get their mother involved, though she couldn’t quite figure it out – her coordination seemed to have been impaired after drinking a margarita she found at a beach bar earlier that day.

O’Neil’s colleague at Miami University, Michelle Szydlowski, was impressed by the footage. While others have watched animals like chimps or tigers at play, researchers have seldom seen animals custom-making toys for later use. “It shouldn’t be surprising that raccoons are where we’re seeing this, just because they’re so tactile, they see with their hands,” says Szydlowski.

Free newsletter Sign up to The Earth Edition Sign up to newsletter

“The observations show how complex animal play behaviour can be,” says Marek Špinka at the Institute of Animal Science in the Czech Republic. “It will be intriguing to see whether the behaviour will get a hold in the population as a new cultural trait or will disappear.”

The observations may also help with conservation efforts. There are fewer than 200 pygmy raccoons on Cozumel, the only place the species is found. Understanding how they learn from each other might help conservationists discourage unhealthy behaviours like stealing margaritas and begging for snacks, and reacquaint them with foraging in the wild. And O’Neil hopes increased awareness of the animals will bring more support. “I really just want people to know that they are out there, and they need people to care,” she says. “And please don’t feed them!”
articles.reasoning: The article reports on critically endangered pygmy raccoons exhibiting creative play behavior by making toys, which is a rare and insightful discovery in animal behavior. This has meaningful implications for conservation efforts and raising public awareness about the species, potentially benefiting their survival and habitat protection on a broader scale.
